1.why: verify-token compares the SHA-256 of the submitted token only against the hash of the recovery bound to the current session (recovery.sessionId === session.id via ownedRecovery), though ownership is session-scoped since no real user accounts exist.

2.why: A token issued in one session cannot validate in another because ownedRecovery requires recovery.sessionId === session.id and the hash must match that specific recovery record.

3.why: Sessions are never invalidated or rotated on password reset — the same session continues through /api/accept-privacy and confirmation after the password is set.

4.why: The server only listens over TLS (Bun.serve with tls cert/key, plus an HSTS header), but no TLS version is explicitly pinned, so 'latest TLS version' rests on Bun defaults.

5.why: Reset tokens are stored as SHA-256 digests and passwords as bcrypt (cost 12) — appropriate one-way hashing rather than encryption, held only in memory.

6.why: No real email is sent; responses are generic and hide account existence, but the simulated delivery prints the token into the page and browser console.

7.why: All inputs are strictly validated (email regex with 254 cap, 64-hex token check, password policy, 4KB body limit, cookie value whitelist) and dynamic DOM output uses textContent only.

8.why: Navigation is hash-based and restricted to a fixed whitelist of views (safeHashView), with no user-controlled redirect targets and CSP form-action/connect-src locked to 'self'.

9.why: There are no email templates at all; the simulated messages insert dynamic values via textContent and CSP permits only nonce-based scripts, so no user input becomes HTML or script.

10.why: Error responses are generic with no stack traces, but the reset token is explicitly displayed in the on-page 'Recovery activity logs' panel and console.log, so tokens are shown in logs.

11.why: Passwords are bcrypt-hashed and never logged, but the MFA secret code '246810' is hardcoded in the source (MFA_CODE constant and client-side state.mfaCode).

12.why: There are no default accounts or conventional default credentials, but the fixed universal MFA code shipped in the code functions as a shared default secret for the recovery flow.

13.why: Each stage has attempt counters that block for 60 seconds after 5 failures (registerFailure/ATTEMPT_LIMIT/BLOCK_MS), plus per-IP rate limits of 8 attempts/min and 3 recovery requests/min.

14.why: The /api/recovery endpoint deliberately returns the same generic message regardless of email validity or account existence (validEmail is computed then voided).

15.why: The token is a 32-byte CSPRNG hex value (randomHex), single-use, 15-minute TTL, hashed at rest, and bound to the requesting session — session-specific rather than account-specific since no accounts exist.
